knowledge_graph.title: Epstein–Barr virus
knowledge_graph.description: The Epstein–Barr virus, also known as human herpesvirus 4, is one of the nine known human herpesvirus types in the herpes family, and is one of the most common viruses in humans. EBV is a double-stranded DNA virus. EBV is the first identified oncogenic virus, a virus that can cause cancer.

related_questions.question: What are the symptoms of Epstein-Barr virus?

text_blocks.snippet: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) commonly causes infectious mononucleosis, which presents with symptoms like fatigue, fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes. Other potential symptoms include an enlarged spleen or liver, and sometimes a rash. While many children experience no or mild symptoms, teenagers and adults often have a more noticeable illness with symptoms lasting weeks or even months.
snippet_highlighted_words: fatigue, fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes

list.snippet: Fatigue: Extreme tiredness or exhaustion, which can be prolonged.
Fever: Elevated body temperature.
Sore Throat: Inflammation and pain in the throat.
Swollen Lymph Nodes: Enlarged lymph nodes, especially in the neck, often described as "swollen glands".
Enlarged Spleen or Liver: These organs can become swollen as part of the body's response to the virus.
Rash: A skin rash may also occur.

list.title: Severity Varies:
list.snippet: Symptoms can range from mild and unnoticed to severe and debilitating, especially in teenagers and adults.

list.title: Duration:
list.snippet: While many people recover within a few weeks, some experience prolonged fatigue or other symptoms for months.

list.title: Reactivation:
list.snippet: EBV can become dormant in the body and reactivate later, potentially without causing symptoms.

list.title: Contagious:
list.snippet: Even when asymptomatic, EBV can be spread to others through saliva and other bodily fluids.

text_blocks.snippet: No, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) does not go away. Once a person is infected with EBV, it remains in the body for life, becoming dormant (inactive). While the virus typically becomes inactive and doesn't cause further issues, it can reactivate under certain conditions, potentially leading to symptoms.
snippet_highlighted_words: No, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) does not go away

list.title: Dormancy:
list.snippet: After the initial infection, EBV becomes dormant in the body's B lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell).

list.title: Reactivation:
list.snippet: EBV can reactivate, meaning it can become active again and potentially cause symptoms.

list.title: Triggers:
list.snippet: Reactivation can be triggered by factors like stress, a weakened immune system, or other infections.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: When EBV reactivates, it may or may not cause noticeable symptoms. Individuals with weakened immune systems are more likely to experience symptoms during reactivation.

list.title: No Cure:
list.snippet: There isn't a cure for EBV infection, but treatments can help manage symptoms.

list.title: Contagious:
list.snippet: Even when dormant, EBV can be spread through saliva, and reactivation can make someone contagious again, even if they don't have symptoms.

related_questions.question: What does an EBV flare feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: An Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) flare, also known as a reactivation, can feel like a return of symptoms similar to those experienced during the initial infection, or it can be milder. Common symptoms include fatigue, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, fever, and headaches. In some cases, there may also be a rash, enlarged spleen or liver, and muscle aches. The severity and duration of symptoms can vary greatly.
snippet_highlighted_words: a return of symptoms similar to those experienced during the initial infection, or it can be milder

text_blocks.snippet: More specifically, a flare might feel like:

list.snippet: Intense fatigue: This can be debilitating and last for weeks or even months.
A sore throat that doesn't improve: It may be accompanied by swollen tonsils and difficulty swallowing.
Swollen and tender lymph nodes: These are often found in the neck, armpits, and groin.
Fever and chills: These can fluctuate in intensity.
Headaches and body aches: These can range from mild to severe.
Skin rashes: Some individuals may develop a rash during a flare-up.
Enlarged spleen or liver: These may cause discomfort or pain in the abdomen.
EBV can reactivate, especially if the immune system is weakened.
Symptoms can be similar to other illnesses, so it's important to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.
While most people recover from EBV within a few weeks or months, some may experience lingering fatigue or recurring symptoms.

related_questions.question: What triggers EBV reactivation?
related_questions.snippet: EBV never truly goes away. Even if the symptoms subside, the virus will remain inactive inside your body until it is reactivated by a trigger. Some triggers include stress, a weakened immune system, taking immunosuppressants, or hormonal changes such as menopause.
